appraisal_events.evidence: « Le petit a l'air fatigué, il devrait monter se coucher » ; « laisse ta mère, vous vous êtes assez dit bonsoir comme cela, ces manifestations sont ridicules » ; « il me fallut partir sans viatique » ; Françoise judges him « un aussi petit personnage que moi » ; the letter to maman ends with « Il n'y a pas de réponse ».
appraisal_events.explanation: The dominant body of the passage stages the boy's exclusion from the valued space of the dinner and the loss of the goodnight kiss: he is dismissed by grandfather and father, ranked below the guest by Françoise's code, reduced to a lie and a ruse, and then flatly refused by his mother. The closing resolve to wait up brings relief and resolve, not realized intimacy, so it does not reverse the local movement.

appraisal_events.evidence: « Il n'y a pas que M. Vinteuil qui ait des voisins aimables », s'écria ma tante Céline ... tout en jetant sur Swann ce qu'elle appelait un regard significatif ; then « Comment ? vous admirez cela ? Eh bien ! c'est du joli ! ... Mais c'est abominable, tout simplement. Et vous osez citer cela ? » — « Swann interloqué », « Swann étonné », « elle le croyait sur la sellette ».
appraisal_events.explanation: Céline's oblique thanks and then her public moral reproof put Swann on the spot and wreck the grandfather's attempt to draw him out. The narration plainly ironizes her (her voice is « factice », her ear is anesthetised except at the word Saint-Simon, and the grandfather answers with « Seigneur, que de vertus vous nous faites haïr ! »), so the snub checks Swann in the moment while telling against her.

status_effects.explanation: He is deprived of the kiss, forced into a humiliating stratagem, and then refused outright; his anxiety is the passage's governing movement.
He is sent up before dinner and shut out of the « salle à manger interdite, hostile » where the others, and his mother, remain with the guest.
Her contrived allusion and indignant tirade expose her as obtuse and self-righteous; the narration and the grandfather's exasperation put her clearly in the wrong.

Repeatedly interrupted and left « interloqué », Swann cannot carry his Saint-Simon anecdote through, so his conversational command is checked within the scene even though the narration sides with him.
The refusal « Il n'y a pas de réponse » confirms that she holds the leverage the boy craves, and her aside to Swann is framed as a delicate gain wrung from constraint.

ambiguities: The great-aunt (« ma tante », « ma grand'tante ») is the passage's most active evaluator — she deflates Swann's Figaro honour, rebukes the grandmother, and is analysed by the narrator as converting envy into pity — but she is unnamed and absent from the reference sheet, so her appraisals are recorded only through their targets. The bare « ma tante » of the first sentence is fixed to her, not to tante Léonie, by the « répondit ma grand'tante » that follows.

The aunts' attitude to Swann is explicitly left undetermined by the narrator: Flora's look is « mêlé de congratulation et d'ironie », and the text offers three alternative motives (« soit simplement pour souligner le trait d'esprit de sa sœur, soit qu'elle enviât Swann de l'avoir inspiré, soit qu'elle ne pût s'empêcher de se moquer de lui »), so it is genuinely underdetermined whether the aunts' behaviour is grateful, envious, or mocking.
